blocks.content: Drainage system and rivers form one of the most important chapters of Physical Geography.
Rivers are dynamic agents of erosion, transportation, and deposition and play a crucial role in

shaping the Earth’s surface. The drainage system refers to the network of rivers and streams in a given area. This chapter is extremely important for  examinations because questions are frequently asked on drainage patterns, river courses, river landforms, and river-based terms.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Drainage patterns are classified into Dendritic, Trellis, Radial, Rectangular, and Centripetal based on slope, underlying rock structure, and climate.
A drainage basin refers to the total geographical area drained by a river and its tributaries, divided from adjacent basins by a watershed.
A river progresses through three distinct stages: the Upper Course (dominated by erosion), the Middle Course (transportation & meanders), and the Lower Course (deposition).
River landforms are divided into Erosional Landforms (such as V-shaped valleys, gorges, and waterfalls) and Depositional Landforms (such as deltas, floodplains, and alluvial fans).

blocks.content: Drainage system refers to the arrangement or pattern of rivers and streams in a region. It is influenced by factors such as slope of land, rock structure, geological history, and climatic conditions.

A drainage basin is the area drained by a river and its tributaries. The boundary separating one drainage basin from another is called a watershed or water divide. Watersheds are usually formed by ridges or highlands.
The development of a drainage system depends on slope, nature of rocks, geological structure, climate, and tectonic activity. Hard rocks resist erosion, while soft rocks are eroded easily.
Dendritic drainage pattern resembles the branches of a tree. It develops on homogeneous rock structures with gentle slopes. It is the most common drainage pattern.
Trellis drainage pattern develops in regions with alternating hard and soft rock layers. Main rivers flow parallel to each other, and tributaries join at right angles.
Radial drainage pattern develops around volcanic cones or dome-shaped uplands. Streams flow outward in all directions from a central high point.
Rectangular drainage pattern develops in regions with jointed or faulted rocks. Streams follow the joints and faults, forming right-angle bends.
Centripetal drainage pattern is characterized by streams flowing inward toward a central depression or basin, such as inland lakes or deserts.

A river is a natural flowing stream of water that moves from higher elevation to lower elevation under the influence of gravity. Rivers originate from glaciers, springs, lakes, or rainfall and ultimately drain into seas, oceans, or inland basins.

The upper course of a river is characterized by steep gradient and dominant erosion. Vertical erosion is prominent, resulting in the formation of V-shaped valleys, gorges, interlocking spurs, waterfalls, and rapids.
In the middle course, the gradient becomes gentle and lateral erosion increases. The river widens its valley and forms meanders, river cliffs, and floodplains.
The lower course has a very gentle slope and deposition becomes dominant. The river deposits sediments to form extensive floodplains, levees, oxbow lakes, deltas, and distributaries.
River erosional landforms include V-shaped valleys, gorges, canyons, waterfalls, rapids, potholes, and river cliffs.

items: Match-the-following questions often pair drainage patterns with examples (e.g., Radial pattern in the Amarkantak range, Dendritic in northern plains).
Questions frequently distinguish between Erosional (Gorges, Canyons, Waterfalls) vs Depositional (Deltas, Oxbow Lakes, Levees) landforms.
Conceptual questions commonly test the exact difference between a Drainage Basin and a Watershed line.

blocks.content: River depositional landforms include floodplains, natural levees, meanders, oxbow lakes, deltas, and alluvial plains.

Tributary is a stream that joins the main river. Distributary is a branch of a river that flows away from the main channel. Confluence is the point where two rivers meet. River mouth is the place where a river enters a sea or lake.
Rivers are lifelines of human civilization. They provide water for drinking, irrigation, industries, hydroelectric power, transportation, and fertile soil for agriculture.
